doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Charlie Parker sitting in at Tin Pan Alley and Gibbs tying his shoe
summary: Bird borrowed money promising to sit in; he showed up at Georgie Auld's Tin Pan Alley and Gibbs stalled by tying his shoe rather than follow him; remarks on Giant Steps tempo.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Okay. I understand that Charlie Parker, in order to borrow money would sometimes promise to show up on your gig. Is that correct?

Yes. Well he did — not me. He did show up on my job, this is when I was just learning bebop of which unfortunately he showed up and scared the hell out of me. If you notice where I write in my book that first of all you’d walk down to Birdland and he’d be standing there and he’d say, “Give me a quarter” or “give me a half dollar.” That was a lot of money in those days. And, and these musicians would say, “I don’t have it.” And he’d say, “Where are you playing tomorrow I’ll come and sit in with you.” And they gave him the money and people would — word would get out, “Bird’s going to come and sit in.” He never would show up. He never would know who you were. But I had a great rapport with Bird. The first thing I did was tell him off after he asked me for some money, I said, “You’re the greatest musician in the world begging and all that.” I really let him know it. And then he said, “Where are you playing tomorrow?” I said, “Over at Georgie Auld’s Tin Pan Alley.” And I gave him a dollar. You know I mean I knew he never showed up. The place was packed when I got to work. We were the first sixteen bars and out of nowhere I saw him and I’m playing the melody and all of a sudden he walks in with one of his plastic horns around and he came and played the next sixteen bars and he’s standing next to me now. Now, once again, as I write in my book if you ask me would I rather follow him playing and then stop playing or fight Mike Tyson? Mike Tyson, one punch I’m out that’s the end of it. Here I’ve got to stand here while he plays 30 choruses and where I come in to play trying not to play anything he just played you know? And so what I did, because as I mentioned in the book, what I did on the 30th bar,

it was only a 32 bar chorus. On the 30th bar, because I knew I wanted to see him go into another chorus, I bent down to tie my shoe. I was on the floor. When he started to play more I got up so then when the 30 bars came closer to 30 bars I went down and tied my shoe. And then once again I had loosened my vibes, I had tied them down — I didn’t know what I was doing. But after about 16 choruses on the floor, my piano player who didn’t think he was even going to follow him because I would come in next, got panicked how he looked at me on the floor like he’s having a nervous breakdown, he says, “I know what you’re doing if you think I’m going to follow him you’re crazy.” We were almost like a bunch of scared little kids. You know Charlie Parker was so far ahead of everybody. You know there’s a record of “Cherokee” of him playing years ago at somebody’s house with just guitar playing at that fluid tempo. You know sometimes playing fast tempos can be on a song with a lot of chord changes, like for example “Giant Steps” that was done very fast. And you can get away by playing a chromatic scale on that song. Because every two beats is a different chord change. Every two beats. Well Buddy DeFranco and I recorded it at a slower tempo and it was harder to play because then you’ve got to make sense of all the notes, you know? And Milt Jackson, I think that’s the first time he ever said anything nice about me. He reviewed the record and he said, “Now that’s the tempo it should have been out and Terry sounded good.”
At that point, about that time with the Charlie Parker incident were you in your early twenties?
Oh yeah I had just got out of the Army. It could have been about 1940 — I left the Army in 1940, I was about 24.
